University of Liverpool, Liverpool, United Kingdom PRESENTING AUTHOR Myra Okumu BACKGROUND Environmental surveillance (ES) of wastewater and rivers provides a cost-effective, population-level approach to pathogen detection with potential to inform vaccine deployment and impact evaluation. Shigella has been detected in environmental waters; however, it remains unclear whether environmental detection correlates with clinical shigellosis incidence or captures circulating species and serotypes. METHODS We implemented ES alongside the Enterics for Global Health (EFGH) hybrid Shigella clinical surveillance study in Ndirande, Blantyre (~103,000 residents) which drains into the Mudi River. Weekly samples were collected from nine river sites and one defunct wastewater treatment plant (n=530). Shigella-positive samples underwent speciation and serotyping using the same multiplex qPCR assays as EFGH clinical diagnostics, enabling direct comparison. RESULTS ipaH was detected in 22.1% of grab samples and 42.1% of Moore swabs. Mixed-effects regression using ipaH copy number from unenriched grab samples showed a statistically significant positive association with clinical incidence. S. sonnei was detected in only 3.1% of ES samples, indicating marked discordance requiring further investigation. Serotype resolution for S. flexneri was limited by mixed environmental populations; however, S. flexneri 6, the second most common clinical serotype, was detectable via a unique PCR target (29.7% Moore swab positivity). CONCLUSION Data suggests ES reflects population-level Shigella burden, though serotype-level detection requires further validation before ES can be used to guide vaccine introduction. If concordance between environmental and clinical serotype distributions is confirmed, ES could serve as a scalable, low-cost tool to monitor vaccine impact without reliance on facility-based surveillance alone. abstracts.researchProblem: Vaccine impact depends on vaccination coverage. However, traditional
abstracts.plainConclusion: These findings shows the synergetic potential of machine-learning approaches and serology data as a complementary tool for objective evaluation of vaccine uptake, to help the interpretation of vaccine impact data for research and programmatic settings where traditional coverage estimates are uncertain.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
INTRODUCTION
Vaccine impact depends on vaccination coverage. However, traditional methods for estimating vaccine coverage, such as administrative data and post-campaign coverage surveys, are often limited by documentation challenges including incomplete data and recall or reporting bias from caregivers. In this study, we used verified serology training datasets to objectively assess post-campaign Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine (TCV) coverage in children from Blantyre, Malawi.
METHODS
Supervised machine learning approaches (Elastic net logistic regression (ENLR), random forest (RF) and support vector machines (SVM)) were trained on anti-Vi IgG concentrations while adjusting for age, sex and antibody decay over time, using a training data set (with known TCV vaccination status) from a TCV immunogenicity trial. Subsequently, the trained models were applied to predict unknown vaccination status in healthy children recruited under the Sero-surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in Malawi study.
RESULTS
In the training dataset, Vi IgG levels were significantly higher among the vaccinated children than the unvaccinated children (p<0.001); and classification performance was consistently high (accuracy>94%) in all three models. In the application data, predicted vaccination coverage ranged from 47% (95% CI: 44%-50% for ENLR and RF) to 52% (95% CI 49%-55% for SVM), which is consistent with the MITIMA study surveillance estimate (47%), but significantly lower than previous programmatic national estimates.
CONCLUSION
These findings highlight the synergetic potential of machine-learning approaches and serology data as a complementary tool for objective evaluation of vaccine uptake, to facilitate the interpretation of vaccine impact data for research and programmatic settings where traditional coverage estimates are uncertain.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
RTS,S/AS01, Streptococcus pneumoniae, antimicrobial resistance, pneumococcal carriage, vaccines
INTRODUCTION
RTS,S/AS01 vaccination reduces clinical malaria, a major cause of febrile illness and driver of antibiotic use promoting the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in sub-Saharan Africa. We leveraged an existing cluster-randomised evaluation of RTS,S/AS01 in Malawi to investigate the vaccine effects on carriage of antimicrobial resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, a key bystander pathogen, for evidence of beneficial vaccine effects on AMR.
METHODS
Three cross-sectional surveys were conducted between 2022 and 2024 corresponding to 2.5, 3, and 3.5 years from vaccine introduction. The study was conducted across two clusters, RTS,S/AS01-exposed and unexposed, in Mangochi District, Malawi. A total of 2100 children aged 15-24 months were enrolled (700 children per survey). From randomly selected households, 707 and 679 pneumococcal isolates from RTS,S/AS01 exposed and unexposed children respectively, were selected for whole genome sequencing. Adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR) by exposure status were estimated using modified Poisson regression adjusted for age and survey round.
RESULTS
Overall, pneumococcal carriage was ~67%, with ~19% vaccine-type (VT) carriage. RTS,S/AS01 exposure was associated with lower resistance rates across commonly prescribed antibiotics: penicillin resistance (aPR 0.89, 95% CI 0.84-0.94; p<0.001), erythromycin resistance (aPR 0.78, 95% CI 0.69-0.89; p<0.001), and tetracycline resistance (aPR 0.82, 95% CI 0.74-0.90; p<0.001) and multidrug resistance (MDR) (aPR 0.76, 95% CI 0.65-0.88; p<0.001), among vaccinated children.
CONCLUSION
RTS,S/AS01 vaccination was associated with reduced pneumococcal antimicrobial resistance, suggesting potential indirect benefits beyond malaria prevention.

abstracts.Abstract title: GENOMIC SURVEILLANCE OF SALMONELLA TYPHI BEFORE AND AFTER TYPHOID CONJUGATE VACCINE ROLLOUT IN MALAWI
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Salmonella Typhi; typhoid conjugate vaccine; genomics; antimicrobial resistance; Malawi
BACKGROUND
Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi), the causative agent of typhoid fever, remains a major public health challenge in many low- and middle-income countries. Malawi introduced typhoid conjugate vaccines (TCV) in May 2023. We investigated short-term genomic changes in circulating S. Typhi following TCV introduction.
METHODS
We conducted Illumina whole-genome sequencing of S. Typhi isolates collected from Malawian children enrolled in a Phase 3 randomised controlled trial (2018-2022) and the subsequent longitudinal surveillance study, MITIMA (2022- 2025). We compared S. Typhi lineages, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants, mutations in Vi capsule-associated genes (the viaB locus), and phylogenetic relationships between TCV and MenA vaccine arms as well as between the pre- and post-TCV rollout periods.
RESULTS
We generated high-quality genomes for 337 S. Typhi isolates (136 trial, 201 MITIMA). Most isolates (331/337; 98%) belonged to lineage 4.3.1.1 (H58) while the remaining isolates belonged to lineages 2.2, 3.3.1 and 4.1.1. Phylogenetic analysis showed no clear phylogenetic separation by vaccine group or surveillance period. All H58 isolates carried resistance determinants for ampicillin, cotrimoxazole, and chloramphenicol while the non-H58 isolates were pan-sensitive. Quinolone resistance-associated mutations were detected in nine isolates (gyrA S83F, n=4; gyrB S464F, n=5). Vi capsule-associated mutations were identified in 31/337 (9%) isolates. CONCLUSIONS No genomic differences were found between TCV and MenA vaccine groups or between the pre- and post-TCV rollout periods. These findings suggest no detectable short-term evolutionary impact of TCV on circulating S. Typhi populations. Continued genomic surveillance is needed to assess longer-term vaccine-driven changes.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Salmonella, Malaria, Systems Serology, Age and Antibody Effector Functions
BACKGROUND
Repeated asymptomatic non-typhoidal Salmonella stool exposure is thought to drive natural immune priming through gradual acquisition of protective antibodies. Invasive disease is associated with susceptibility factors, particularly age and malaria infection. Despite this, the quality and functional capacity of naturally acquired antibody responses remain poorly defined.
AIM
To characterize humoral immune responses against iNTS disease and determine how age and malaria infection influence their breadth and functionality.
METHODS
We used systems serology to analyse 350 age-stratified samples (0-5 years), paired at day 0 and 90, from a randomly selected community cohort in Chikwawa, who were characterised by Salmonella stool-exposure and malaria RDT. Antibody isotypes, subclasses, Fc receptor expression, and functional activity (complement fixation, and neutrophil and monocytic phagocytosis) were measured. Mechanistic depletion/inhibitory experiments evaluated IgM, Fc-gamma-R receptor, and complement contributions.
RESULTS
Asymptomatic Salmonella exposure induced antigen-specific IgG1, IgG2, and IgM responses together with complement-activating activity. Antibody responses matured progressively with age. Malaria-positive children exhibited mildly reduced Salmonella-specific IgG, IgM, and Fc-mediated responses, but conversely showed brisk polyclonal activation against non-Salmonella antigens. IgM depletion, Fc-gamma-R blockade, and complement inactivation significantly reduced complement binding and phagocytic activity, regardless of malaria status but differentially by age.
CONCLUSION
Naturally acquired immunity to Salmonella is characterized by agedependent maturation and depends on coordinated IgG-, IgM-, Fc receptor-, and complement-mediated mechanisms. Malaria selectively modulates these responses, providing insights into susceptibility to iNTS disease. Vaccine responses in young children would ideally produce broadly functional responses, mirroring those in naturally protected older children.

abstracts.Abstract title: RESPIRATORY SYNCYTIAL VIRUS INFECTION AND AGE-SPECIFIC SEROLOGY IN YOUNG CHILDREN IN BLANTYRE, MALAWI
abstracts.actualAbstract:
BACKGROUND
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading viral cause of acute respiratory infection in young children and a key target for emerging prevention strategies, including maternal vaccination and long-acting monoclonal antibodies. Community-based data on RSV subtype distribution and serological responses in Malawian children are needed to define disease burden and inform prevention strategies.
METHODS
We analysed samples from 527 children aged 0-24 months attending primary healthcare clinics in three urban communities in Blantyre, Malawi, between January 2024 and December 2025. Children with acute respiratory symptoms and asymptomatic children were included. Samples were tested by RT-qPCR for RSV detection and subtype identification. RSV-specific IgG against crude RSV A2 antigen was measured by ELISA. Age-specific IgG trends were modelled using generalised additive models and locally estimated scatterplot smoothing.
RESULTS
RSV was detected in 37/527 children (7.0%; 95% CI 5.0-9.5%). RSV-A accounted for 23/37 (62.2%) infections and RSV-B for 14/37 (37.8%). Among RSV-positive children, upper respiratory tract infection was most common (27/37, 73.0%), with pneumonia in 3/37 (8.1%) and bronchiolitis in 1/37 (2.7%); the remainder were asymptomatic or had other diagnoses. RSV-specific IgG was undetectable in 70.3% (26/37) of RSV-positive children compared with 228/490 (46.5%) of RSV-negative children. IgG levels reached a nadir at 8.7 months of age. CONCLUSIONS These data define a discrete early-life susceptibility window in urban Malawian children and support prioritisation of maternal vaccination or long-acting monoclonal antibodies prior to this period. They provide community-based evidence from a low-resource setting to guide timing and establish a baseline for evaluating future RSV prevention strategies.

abstracts.Abstract title: THE IMPACT OF MALARIA RTS,S/AS01 VACCINE AND PCV-13 ON EXTENDED-SPECTRUM BETA-LACTAMASE (ESBL)- PRODUCING ESCHERICHIA COLI CARRIAGE AND ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE IN MALAWIAN CHILDREN
abstracts.plainConclusion: RTS,S/AS01 vaccination reduced ESBL-Ec carriage independent of AMU, suggesting a non-antimicrobial pathway. The underlying causal pathways require further investigation to maximise the potential for RTS,S/AS01 vaccination to provide population-level AMR control.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Vaccination, Antimicrobial Resistance, ESBL-producing E. coli
BACKGROUND
Sub-Saharan Africa bears a high burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), driven partly by empirical antimicrobial use (AMU) for febrile illness, which selects for Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec), a WHO priority pathogen. Vaccines may reduce AMR directly or indirectly by lowering antibiotic exposure, but evidence from low-income settings is limited. We assessed associations between RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccination, PCV13 vaccination schedules, and ESBL-Ec carriage among Malawian children. METHODOLOGY We analysed data from two cluster-randomised vaccine evaluations in Malawi: the RTS,S/AS01 Malaria Vaccine Implementation Programme in Mangochi (vaccinated versus unvaccinated clusters) and a PCV13 schedule study in Blantyre (2P+1 versus 3P+0 dosing schedules in six clusters). Children aged 15-24 months were recruited through three cross-sectional household surveys. Stool samples were screened for ESBL-Ec. Vaccine exposure and antimicrobial use were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression adjusting for confounders. Whole-genome sequencing compared resistance genes and bacterial lineages between vaccine groups.
RESULTS
RTS,S/AS01 vaccination was associated with 45% lower odds of ESBL-Ec carriage (aOR = 0.55, 95% CI: 0.40-0.75; p < 0.001). There was no association with PCV-13 schedule (aOR = 1.07, 95% CI: 0.72-1.58; p = 0.747). Neither vaccine exposure was associated with a significant change in AMU. ESBL-Ec resistance genes and sequence types did not differ across vaccine groups.
CONCLUSION
RTS,S/AS01 vaccination reduced ESBL-Ec carriage independent of AMU, suggesting a non-antimicrobial pathway. The underlying causal pathways require further investigation to maximise the potential for RTS,S/AS01 vaccination to provide population-level AMR control.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
BACKGROUND
Effective tools for detecting pneumococcal serotypes from urine could strengthen pneumonia surveillance in high-burden settings. The 24-plex serotype-specific urine antigen detection assay (24ssUAD), developed by the UK Health Security Agency, is a laboratory-based assay. Although it performs well in UK adults, its utility in high pneumococcal carriage settings remains unclear.
METHODS
We evaluated pneumococcal polysaccharide shedding in urine among 214 children aged 1-4 years hospitalised with acute respiratory infection at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, Malawi (2016-2019). Caregiver-reported antibiotic exposure within seven days was recorded, and urine antibiotic activity was measured. Nasopharyngeal carriage was assessed by culture of nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS) and 63 urines underwent 24ssUAD testing. To contextualise detection patterns, we examined urine from 47 Malawian adults inoculated with Streptococcus pneumoniae serotype 3 or 6B in a controlled human infection model. Samples were collected at baseline and post-inoculation visits to day 28.
RESULTS
24ssUAD detected pneumococcal serotypes in 72.4% (155/214) of children, including serotypes 1, 5, 3, 4, and 9N rarely detected by NPS-culture. Antibiotic exposure was reported in 35.5% (76/214), with 71.4% (45/63) showing urine antibiotic activity. Detection by 24ssUAD was unaffected by antibiotic use (72.4% vs 72.5%; p=0.55), whereas NPS culture positivity declined from 85.7% to 20.5% with antibiotic use (p<0.001). Findings from the controlled human infection model supported these observations, with urinary antigen detected after serotype 3 colonisation but not after serotype 6B colonisation, suggesting serotype-dependent urinary antigen shedding.
CONCLUSION
24ssUAD detected pneumococcal serotypes in children despite high antibiotic exposure, and adult shedding patterns highlight serotype-dependent variability. The assay shows potential for pneumococcal surveillance in high-burden settings, though further evaluation is required.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
INTRODUCTION
Invasive nontyphoidal salmonellosis (iNTS) and typhoid fever are major public health concerns in resource-limited settings. S. Enteritidis and S. Typhimurium account for >90% of iNTS cases. A novel trivalent iNTS-TCV vaccine is under development by the GSK Vaccines Institute for Global Health (GVGH).
METHODS
In Stage 1, 50 European adults were randomized (2:2:1) to receive either iNTS-TCV + saline, iNTS-GMMA + TCV, or placebo + saline, as separate intramuscular injections in opposite arms on Days 1, 57, and 169. In Stage 2, 105 African adults were randomized (3:3:1) to receive iNTS-TCV + saline, iNTS-GMMA + TCV (full doses), or active comparators (Menveo + saline, Boostrix + saline, or Typhim Vi + saline) on the same schedule.
RESULTS
Most unsolicited adverse events were mild-to-moderate, unrelated to vaccination, and resolved within 7 days. For the S. Typhi component, Vi-specific IgG responses peaked 28 days after the first dose and were similar between vaccine groups, with no further boosting after subsequent doses. IgG responses to S. Typhimurium and S. Enteritidis O-antigens also increased after the first dose, with no additional boosting. Functional antibody responses in Europe increased after the first dose without further boosting. In Africa, where baseline titres were higher, a similar pattern was observed for S. Typhimurium, while high baseline bactericidal activity for S. Enteritidis limited detection of vaccine-induced increases. CONCLUSIONS The vaccine induced antibodies against all three target antigens, with no evidence of immune interference with the TCV component, supporting further investigation in the target population.

abstracts.Abstract title: DRIVERS OF FINE-SCALE SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL VARIATION IN MALARIA AND SCHISTOSOMIASIS IN CHIKWAWA, MALAWI: A GENERALIZED ADDITIVE MODELLING STUDY
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Malaria; Urogenital schistosomiasis; Spatial GAMs; Co-infection; Hotspot mapping
BACKGROUND
Malaria and urogenital schistosomiasis remain co-endemic in southern Malawi, but the drivers of fine-scale spatial variation in transmission are poorly understood. Most studies rely on aggregated data or school locations, obscuring local heterogeneity and limiting geographically targeted interventions. We investigated the environmental, demographic, and behavioural determinants of malaria and urogenital schistosomiasis at sub-district scale in Chikwawa District, Malawi.
METHODS
We analysed village-level data from four repeated cross-sectional school-based surveys (September 2023 - March 2025) involving 4,176 school-aged children from 21 primary schools. Participants' villages were geolocated, enabling community-level rather than school-level analyses. Spatial generalized additive models (GAMs) quantified non-linear relationships between infection risk and environmental, demographic, and behavioural factors while accounting for residual spatial dependence.
RESULTS
Spatial GAMs outperformed non-spatial models, confirming substantial finescale spatial heterogeneity. Malaria risk decreased with elevation (p=0.006) but increased with surface water coverage (p=0.031), older age (p=0.001), and urogenital schistosomiasis co-infection (OR=1.53, p=0.003). Predicted malaria risk increased from <10% to ~25% as surface water coverage rose from 0% to 6%. Urogenital schistosomiasis risk was associated with proximity to irrigation infrastructure (p=0.001), greater distance to health facilities (p=0.002), surface water (p=0.015), proximity to water bodies (p=0.023), male sex, water contact, and malaria co-infection. Malaria hotspots occurred mainly in the western lowelevation corridor, whereas schistosomiasis hotspots were concentrated in south-central and eastern communities. CONCLUSIONS Despite district-wide co-endemicity, malaria and urogenital schistosomiasis exhibit distinct fine-scale transmission patterns, while bidirectional coinfection supports integrated screening. Spatial GAMs enable sub-district hotspot identification and can inform geographically targeted, integrated surveillance and control strategies in Malawi.

abstracts.Abstract title: SINGLE-CELL TRANSCRIPTOMICS AND IN-VITRO GENE PERTURBATION EXPERIMENTS REVEAL CANRENONE AS A POTENTIAL HOST-DIRECTED THERAPEUTIC AGENT FOR TUBERCULOSIS
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Tuberculosis, Host-directed therapies, Macrophages
BACKGROUND
The prevalence of drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) is increasing in some parts of the world. Host-directed therapies (HDTs) present a potential avenue for combating drug-resistant TB, yet the optimal drug targets for HDTs remain elusive. OBJECTIVES This study aimed to identify novel host-directed therapies for TB using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and in-vitro gene perturbation experiments.
METHODS
We analyzed scRNA-seq datasets of human monocyte-derived macrophages either exposed or unexposed to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) (GSM2486334 and GSM2486335). Augur was employed to identify cell clusters showing significant transcriptomic changes post-exposure. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was used to identify perturbed biological pathways in the Mtb-exposed macrophages. Next, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) were used to downregulate genes within the perturbed pathways in Mtb-macrophage co-cultures. Finally, Autodock was utilized to predict ligands for the ASO-targeted proteins.
RESULTS
Unsupervised clustering revealed four macrophage clusters. GSEA highlighted enrichment of genes linked to metabolism and vesicle activity in the Mtbexposed cells in the cluster with the highest Augur score. ASOs targeting Coronin-1A, a protein involved in vesicle activity, led to a 40% reduction in bacterial load in Mtbinfected macrophages. Finally, molecular docking predicted Canrenone as a potential ligand for Coronin-1A. CONCLUSIONS This study identified Canrenone as a promising small-molecule modulator of Coronin-1A activity, suggesting its potential as a candidate host-directed therapy for TB. Our future work will involve testing canrenone's antimycobacterial and immunomodulatory activity in Mtb-macrophage co-cultures.

abstracts.Abstract title: GEOSPATIAL METHODS FOR WASTE SURVEILLANCE IN URBAN AFRICAN ENVIRONMENT Patrick K. Kalonde, Kestern Mkoola, Taonga Mwapasa, Richard Quilliam, Kondwani Chidziwisano, Tracy Morse, Nicholas Feasey, Michelle C. Stanton, Peter M. Atkinson, Marc Y. R. Henrion
abstracts.plainConclusion: This work establishes a reproducible framework linking environmental remote sensing with infectious disease epidemiology, opening new avenues for studying human exposure pathways and evaluating waste management interventions.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
One Health; remote sensing; waste management; disease exposure modelling
BACKGROUND
Recent discoveries that unmanaged plastic waste serves as a reservoir for pathogenic bacteria suggest it is an emerging, overlooked One Health concern, particularly where waste management is inadequate. Evidence linking waste piles to pathogen reservoirs and human exposure remains too limited to justify policy change. We aimed to develop methods for mapping waste accumulation, quantify spatio-temporal patterns over a year and develop methods to examine associations with human exposure.
METHODS
Using advances in drone technology, we developed and validated an automated remote sensing pipeline for high resolution mapping of waste accumulations in an urban informal settlement. We applied it monthly from March 2024 to February 2025 in Blantyre, Malawi to characterise spatio-temporal drivers of waste persistence and dispersal. We then developed a novel physics-and-biology-informed exposure metric integrating mapped waste locations with river network topology, and compared it against commonly used metrics, including Euclidean distance, through simulation modelling across a range of transmission scenarios.
RESULTS
The automated U-Net pipeline, which jointly performed segmentation and classification, achieved an F1-score of 0.76 (IoU=0.61), approaching a human-assisted workflow (F1=0.95) and outperforming a fully automated alternative (F1=0.58). Waste accumulations grew in size during the dry season, consistent with reduced dispersal. Against a hypothetical Salmonella Typhi scenario, the novel exposure metric showed promise for identifying exposure risk and at-risk populations, though its advantage over simpler metrics varied by scenario.
CONCLUSION
This work establishes a reproducible framework linking environmental remote sensing with infectious disease epidemiology, opening new avenues for studying human exposure pathways and evaluating waste management interventions.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine; anaemia; perennial malaria chemoprevention; infants; RTS,S/AS01
INTRODUCTION
Perennial malaria chemoprevention (PMC) with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP) can prevent Plasmodium falciparum malaria in infants, but delivery at scale is challenging. Aligning PMC dosing with routine infant health-facility visits may improve feasibility and adherence. We evaluated visit-aligned DP for PMC in Malawian infants during the rollout of RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccination.
METHODS
In this single-blind, placebo-controlled trial (February 2023-February 2025), 220 infants were randomised to a 3-day course of DP or placebo at 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 6 months, and 9 months of age, aligned with routine visits. Malaria parasitaemia was assessed before dosing and 28 days after each course by microscopy and quantitative PCR. Adverse events were monitored to 12 months.
RESULTS
Malaria transmission was low: incidence was 0.001 and 0.004 episodes per person-month in the DP and placebo arms (one and four episodes; 110 infants per arm), all occurring by 7 months of age, when nearly half of infants in both arms had received at least one vaccine dose. DP was associated with a non-significant 77% reduction in malaria incidence (aIRR 0.23, 95% CI 0.03-2.11, p=0.196). After adjustment for vaccine doses received, DP significantly reduced moderate-to-severe anaemia (aRR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52-0.93, p=0.013). Adverse events were comparable between arms (DP 149, placebo 134), with no new safety signal.
CONCLUSION
Visit-aligned DP for PMC was feasible and well tolerated and significantly reduced anaemia, despite low malaria transmission that limited power to detect an effect on incidence. DP may complement RTS,S/AS01 vaccination during early infancy; evaluation in higher-transmission settings is warranted.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Tuberculosis, IGRA (or QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus), Paediatric, HIV, Severe acute malnutrition, IFN-gamma
BACKGROUND
Tuberculosis diagnosis in children under five years (U5s) remains challenging in high-burden settings such as Malawi. The QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) is an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) widely used as part of tuberculosis diagnosis, but its performance in young children, especially those living with HIV or severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is poorly characterised. This study evaluates the performance of the IGRA assay and factors that could influence IGRA
RESULTS
in this group.
METHODS
In an ongoing cohort study of U5s with presumed tuberculosis at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital in Blantyre, 97 participants have been enrolled with IGRA
RESULTS
to date (target n=300). IGRA results are classified as positive, negative, or indeterminate and compared against a microbiological reference standard (MRS: Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra positive) and composite reference standard (CRS). Associations with HIV status, SAM, age and gender were assessed using chi-square and non-parametric tests.
RESULTS
Out of 97 children, six (6.2%) were IGRA-positive, 76 (78.4%) were negative, and 15 (15.5%) had an indeterminate result. Positive IGRA results were significantly associated with CRS (p=0.001) and MRS (p=0.017). Additionally, HIV co-infection was significantly associated with positive IGRA results (p=0.018). Mitogen responses, reflecting overall immune competence, differed significantly by HIV status (p=0.026) and SAM status (p=0.011), and were negatively correlated with age (Spearman's rho=-0.261, p=0.010).
CONCLUSION
Preliminary findings suggest that IGRA results are associated with established TB reference standards, while HIV co-infection influences IGRA results in young Malawian children. The high indeterminate rate represents an important diagnostic limitation. Enrolment is ongoing.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Malaria chemoprevention, transmission modelling, clinical cases, infections
INTRODUCTION
Malawi continues to face a high malaria burden despite the 2030 elimination target, compounded by emerging drug resistance and heterogeneous transmission. The National Malaria Strategic Plan (2023-2030) calls for robust local evidence to guide seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) scale-up, yet in-country mathematical modelling capacity remains limited. We developed a locally calibrated transmission model to identify the most effective SMC drug and coverage strategy.
METHODS
We extended a human-mosquito compartmental transmission model with a chemoprevention compartment incorporating waning protection. The model was calibrated in two stages (Nelder-Mead, then L-BFGS-B) using DHIS and NMCP surveillance data from six districts (Dowa, Kasungu, Mulanje, Mwanza, Mzimba, Salima). Six drugs, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP), sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine (SP+AQ), artemether-lumefantrine, chloroquine, sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, and amodiaquine, were compared under three coverage policies at 80% coverage over a 5-month period. Latin Hypercube Sampling/PRCC identified key sensitivity drivers.
RESULTS
DP averted the highest percentage of both clinical cases and infections across all districts, with clinical aversion ranging from 57% in Dowa to 80% in Kasungu, with SP+AQ performing second-best. Amodiaquine and chloroquine alone were least effective. Mosquito biting rate and treatment rate of infectious humans were the strongest drivers of case counts, with higher biting rates increasing and higher treatment rates reducing cases.
CONCLUSION
We recommend using SP+AQ for SMC because DP is the current firstline treatment. District-level heterogeneity supports tailored, model-informed deployment rather than a uniform national chemoprevention strategy.

abstracts.Abstract title: FROM EVIDENCE TO ACTION: HOW A MULTI-COUNTRY CONSORTIUM LEARNED TO TRANSLATE RESEARCH INTO POLICY AGAINST ANTIMALARIAL DRUG RESISTANCE
abstracts.plainConclusion: Translating evidence into policy within multi-country consortiums depends as much on relationships, trust, and institutional partnerships as on the quality of the evidence. These lessons provide practical insights for strengthening evidence-informed policymaking for complex cross-border health challenges in low- and middle-income countries.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Antimalarial Drug Resistance, Evidence-informed Decision-making, Knowledge Translation, Policy Engagement, Multi-country Consortium
BACKGROUND
Antimalarial drug resistance is an increasing threat to malaria control across southern and eastern Africa. Addressing it requires more than generating high-quality evidence; it also depends on ensuring that evidence informs policy across diverse national and regional contexts. Although evidence-informed decisionmaking is widely promoted, there is limited evidence on how multi-country research consortiums support its implementation in practice. This paper reflects on the experience of an 18-country consortium working to strengthen the policy response to antimalarial drug resistance.
METHODS
We conducted a reflective case study of the consortium's EIDM activities using project documentation, social network analysis (SNA) findings, and practitioner reflections. Lessons were synthesised across five workstreams: policy briefs, webinars, guideline dissemination, country-level technical support, and stakeholder network mapping.
RESULTS
Four lessons emerged. First, trusted data governance enabled cross-country data sharing while preserving national ownership. Second, evidence uptake depended not only on the quality of evidence but also on influential policymakers who championed its use. Third, intentionally leveraging consortium networks extended the reach of research beyond traditional policy audiences. Finally, sustained engagement and trusted relationships proved more influential than one-off knowledge products in supporting policy uptake. Together, these approaches contributed to the East African Community roadmap for antimalarial drug resistance mitigation and a dedicated AMDR chapter in the latest SADC malaria report.
CONCLUSION
Translating evidence into policy within multi-country consortiums depends as much on relationships, trust, and institutional partnerships as on the quality of the evidence. These lessons provide practical insights for strengthening evidence-informed policymaking for complex cross-border health challenges in lowand middle-income countries.

abstracts.Abstract title: COST-EFFECTIVENESS ANALYSIS OF MALARIA CHEMOPREVENTION STRATEGIES IN MALAWI
abstracts.plainConclusion: SP- and AQ-based chemoprevention may offer significant health and economic benefits in Malawi, supporting geographically targeted strategies that consider local transmission, timing, and mortality in economic evaluations.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Malaria, Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention, Cost-effectiveness, Children under five, Malawi
BACKGROUND
Malaria remains a leading cause of illness and death among children under five in Malawi. Despite progress in control, transmission is highly variable across districts. While chemoprevention has proven effective in the Sahel, local evidence on its cost-effectiveness in Malawi is limited. This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of six chemoprevention regimens versus no chemoprevention in six high-burden districts.
METHODS
A model-based cost-effectiveness analysis used outputs from a calibrated SEIR transmission model. Six regimens were assessed: Sulfadoxine Pyrimethamine (SP), Amodiaquine (AQ), Chloroquine (CQ), SP plus AQ (SPAQ), Dihydroartemisinin Piperaquine (DP), and Artemether Lumefantrine (AL). Outcomes included disabilityadjusted life years (DALYs) averted, incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), and return on investment (ROI). Cost-effectiveness was evaluated against Malawi's willingness-to-pay threshold of USD 398.6 per DALY averted. Sensitivity analysis compared district-specific mortality with a standard 1.5% case fatality rate.
RESULTS
SP showed the most favorable economic profile with the lowest ICERs and highest ROI. SP initiated in Salima in December had an ICER of -119.59 USD per DALY averted and ROI of 262.31%. AQ and CQ also showed cost-saving potential in high-burden districts. DP and AL had higher ICERs due to program costs. Results were sensitive to mortality assumptions; observed mortality raised the mean ICER from 8.93 to 292.30 USD per DALY averted.
CONCLUSION
SP- and AQ-based chemoprevention may offer significant health and economic benefits in Malawi, supporting geographically targeted strategies that consider local transmission, timing, and mortality in economic evaluations.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Tuberculosis, Immunoreactivity, Annual Risk of TB Infection (ARTI)
BACKGROUND
Tuberculosis (TB) incidence and mortality are declining in Africa, with transmission concentrating within high-density peri-urban areas. Identifying urban hotspots requires novel epidemiological techniques. By mapping transmission patterns and identifying hotspots, ZAMSA-TB aims to inform the design and evaluation of targeted TB prevention interventions.
METHODS
ZAMSA-TB is a cross-sectional epidemiological survey recruiting healthy children aged 12-60 months in Blantyre, Lusaka, and Cape Town. In Blantyre, 2,369 children recruited from Bangwe, Limbe, and Ndirande Clinics will undergo a baseline questionnaire, geolocation, and interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) testing, with TB care and prevention as required. In preliminary analysis, we estimated MTB immunoreactivity prevalence and annual risk of TB infection, spatial distribution, and compared temporal trends to a previous community-based survey (Timasamala, 2022) completed in the same Blantyre neighbourhoods.
RESULTS
To date, of 672 children recruited, 16 (2.2%) were IGRA-positive, giving an ARTI of 0.89%, which is substantially lower than the 2022 estimate ARTI of 2.7%. Over the 33 small neighbourhoods within the three clusters in 2022, ARTI ranged from 1.11% to 4.11%, whilst the current cluster-level ARTI range is 0.5% to 1.01%.
CONCLUSION
Preliminary findings suggest rapidly declining TB transmission in urban Blantyre over four years, likely due to previous scale-up of antiretroviral therapy for HIV, and TB screening, care, and prevention interventions. ZAMSA-TB shows how MTB immunoreactivity surveillance can provide real-time high-resolution TB surveillance data to direct targeted interventions and evaluate intervention effectiveness.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Antimalarial drug resistance, Chloroquine, Amodiaquine, Marker, sub-Saharan Africa
BACKGROUND
The re-emergence of chloroquine (CQ)-sensitive Plasmodium falciparum following CQ withdrawal has revived discussions on re-introducing CQ alongside concerns over partial artemisinin resistance. Yet, the role of amodiaquine (AQ) in shaping resistance dynamics remains unclear.
METHODS
We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 76 studies following PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251173476). Random-effects meta-analyses estimated the pooled prevalence of P. falciparum chloroquine resistance transporter (Pfcrt K76/K76T), and P. falciparum multidrug resistance marker (pfmdr1) polymorphisms (N86Y, Y184F, and D1246Y), with subgroup analyses using decade and region. Mixed-effects meta-regression assessed effects of AQ policy and temporal trends.
RESULTS
Pooled prevalence of Pfcrt K76 was 70.2% (95% CI: 62.4-77.0), versus 34.9% (95% CI: 28.8-41.7) for the K76T. Sensitivity increased from 10.6% (2000-2010) to >70% after 2015 (p < 0.001), while resistance declined from 80.1% to <35%. Southern Africa showed the highest sensitivity and lowest resistance (7.9%, p = 0.038). Temporal trends were the strongest drivers (beta = -0.1197, p < 0.001); a model including region and AQ policy explained 42% of heterogeneity, though the AQ policy alone was not significant (p = 0.642). Pfmdr1 N86Y declined significantly over time, but no significant trends were observed for Y184F and D1246Y.
CONCLUSION
The expansion and decline of CQ sensitivity and resistance appear temporally associated with CQ withdrawal. Heterogeneous pfmdr1 markers suggest variable drug pressures. Although AQ policy was not significantly associated with Pfcrt prevalence, we cannot exclude haplotype-specific cross-resistance, warranting caution when reconsidering CQ reintroduction in some settings and supporting continued molecular surveillance.

abstracts.Abstract title: MALARIA CHEMOPREVENTION IN SCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL COMPARING DIHYDROARTEMISININ-PIPERAQUINE AND SULFADOXINE-PYRIMETHAMINE PLUS AMODIAQUINE TO CONTROL IN MALAWI
abstracts.plainConclusion: In Malawi and settings with similar malaria transmission and resistance patterns, SPAQ is a suitable non-artemisinin alternative to DP for intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in school children.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
BACKGROUND
School-age children experience a high but underappreciated burden of malaria infection and morbidity. The WHO recommends intermittent preventive treatment for malaria in school-age children (IPTsc), but adoption remains low. Dihydroartemisinin- Piperaquine (DP) has emerged as the drug of choice for IPTsc but due to concerns over artemisinin resistance and restrictions to use of first-line antimalarial treatments for chemoprevention, a non-artemisinin alternative is required.
METHODS
We conducted a randomized controlled trial among primary school children in rural Blantyre, Malawi, who were allocated to the following arms: 1) IPTsc with DP, 2) IPTsc with Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine plus Amodiaquine (SPAQ), and 3) Control (no treatment). During four six-weekly follow-up visits, participants in the treatment arms received full courses of study drugs. Blood specimens for Plasmodium falciparum PCR and haemoglobin were collected at the first intervention visit and at the outcome visit which was done concurrently with the fourth intervention visit. The primary outcome was Pf as detected by PCR. Secondary outcomes included anaemia and clinical malaria.
RESULTS
We enrolled 788 children and obtained primary outcome results for 82% (643) of participants. Among the enrolled, mean age was 9.95 (SD 3.44), 52% were female, and 58% reported sleeping under a bed net. At the outcome, the prevalence of Pf was 3.3% (7/211), 2.9% (6/207) and 12.1% (25/206) in the DP, SPAQ and Control arms respectively. Compared to control, both DP (adjusted OR [aOR]:0.24, 95% CI 0.09-0.55, p=0.001) and SPAQ (aOR 0.22, 95% CI 0.08-0.51, p=0.001) significantly reduced Pf prevalence. Both treatments reduced clinical malaria episodes (DP: aIRR 0.42, 95% CI 0.35-0.51, p<0.001; SPAQ: aIRR 0.39, 95% CI 0.32-0.48, p<0.001). Neither significantly reduced anaemia.
CONCLUSION
In Malawi and settings with similar malaria transmission and resistance patterns, SPAQ is a suitable non-artemisinin alternative to DP for intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in school children.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
INTRODUCTION
Malaria remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in endemic regions, including Malawi. The ABO blood group system has been proposed as a genetic factor influencing disease severity. Evidence suggests that blood group O may confer relative protection against severe malaria; this is attributed to less rosetting, a known driver of cerebral malaria pathogenesis, among erythrocytes of blood type O. Whether this protection extends to other forms of P. falciparum infections requires further elucidation. OBJECTIVES The study aimed to investigate the prevalence of asymptomatic, uncomplicated, and cerebral malaria among these ABO blood phenotypes. Also, peripheral parasitemia and the parasite marker, Histidine-Rich Protein 2 (HRP-2), were used as markers of parasite invasion.
METHODS
A cross-sectional study was conducted involving pediatric patients diagnosed with P. falciparum malaria classified as asymptomatic, uncomplicated, or cerebral. Peripheral parasitemia was quantified by real-time PCR, and plasma levels of HRP-2 were measured by ELISA. ABO blood groups were determined by microplate reverse grouping.
RESULTS
Results showed that children with blood group AB had increased odds of presenting with asymptomatic malaria (OR=2.84, p=0.03) and cerebral malaria (OR=3.57, p=0.004) compared to those with blood group O. Levels of HRP-2 and peripheral parasitemia were similar between asymptomatic and uncomplicated malaria cases, regardless of blood group. However, cerebral malaria cases with blood group O exhibited significantly lower parasitemia and HRP-2 levels compared to other blood groups. CONCLUSIONS These findings support the hypothesis that ABO blood phenotypes influence the severity of P. falciparum infection. They show equal protection provided by blood group O against asymptomatic malaria and cerebral malaria. This protection does not appear to be due to a difference in invasion and is unlikely to be explained by differences in rosetting. Further research is needed to determine the underlying mechanisms responsible for this protection.

abstracts.Abstract title: ANTIGEN-SPECIFIC AND FUNCTIONAL DETERMINANTS OF ANTIBODY RESPONSES TO PfEMP1 IN YOUNG MALAWIAN CHILDREN WITH MALARIA OF VARYING SEVERITY: A SYSTEMS SEROLOGY STUDY

Over half a million children are affected annually, predominantly in sub-Saharan Africa. CM pathogenesis involves the sequestration of P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes (IEs) in the brain's microvasculature, driven by cytoadherence via the antigen PfEMP1. Specific PfEMP1 variants are linked to CM, and antibodies targeting these variants are suggested to correlate with CM protection. Existing research on PfEMP1 immunity across CM, UM, and AP is fragmented, and the types of PfEMP1-specific antibodies associated with protection remain unclear. We aim to identify antigenic PfEMP1 targets and elucidate functional features of antibodies associated with CM protection.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Malaria, Antibodies, PfEMP1, Systems serology
INTRODUCTION
Cerebral malaria (CM), the most severe complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection, leads to coma and the presence of circulating asexual parasites. Over half a million children are affected annually, predominantly in sub-Saharan Africa. CM pathogenesis involves the sequestration of P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes (IEs) in the brain's microvasculature, driven by cytoadherence via the antigen PfEMP1. Specific PfEMP1 variants are linked to CM, and antibodies targeting these variants are suggested to correlate with CM protection. Malaria ranges from asymptomatic parasitaemia (AP) and uncomplicated malaria (UM) to severe syndromes like CM. Immunity to AP and UM may involve antibodies against various PfEMP1 domains, distinct from those linked to CM. Existing research on PfEMP1 immunity across CM, UM, and AP is fragmented, and the types of PfEMP1-specific antibodies associated with protection remain unclear. We aim to identify antigenic PfEMP1 targets and elucidate functional features of antibodies associated with CM protection.
METHODS
We used a systems serology approach, utilising Luminex analysis to compare multiple antibody and Fc receptor responses, including IgG, IgG subclasses, IgA1, and Fc-gamma receptor IIa, IIIa, and IIIb engagement, to 44 PfEMP1 variants in 110 children per group: CM, UM, and AP. Univariable comparisons and multivariable machine learning models were then applied to determine which functional features of antibodies are associated with protection against CM.
RESULTS
We explored more than 300 functional features of antibodies to the different PfEMP1 variants. Preliminary analysis revealed that different antibodies to specific PfEMP1 variants differ across the three groups of participants. Notably, the capacity of PfEMP1-specific antibodies to engage various Fc receptors was more frequently associated with protection from CM than antibody titres alone. Furthermore, we found that PfEMP1-specific antibody responses differentiated AP from UM, suggesting that AP is not merely a presymptomatic stage of infection but a fundamentally distinct serological phenotype.
CONCLUSION
Our findings highlight that antibodies specific to different PfEMP1 variants distinguish between CM, UM, and AP. These results underscore the potential of targeting PfEMP1 variants for augmenting malaria vaccines.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
One Health, transmission, childhood diarrhoea, Campylobacter, risk factors
INTRODUCTION
Campylobacter is a leading cause of diarrhoea in children under five in resource limited settings, where asymptomatic carriage is common and associated with impaired linear growth. This study identifies risk factors for paediatric Campylobacter-associated diarrhoea that have not previously been investigated in Malawi.
METHODS
We conducted a case-control study of children under five years old living in urban Blantyre. Cases were children with Campylobacter-positive diarrhoea (n=48), matched by age and neighbourhood to controls without diarrhoea (n=82) from different households. Questionnaires were administered, and samples collected from household water and environment, plus stools of enrolled children and up to two household members. Campylobacter was detected by culture and PCR. Multivariable analysis, controlling for sex, assessed associations with Campylobacter-associated diarrhoea.
RESULTS
Asymptomatic carriage was detected in 42.68% of control children, and 43.10% of all household members, with carriage independent of age. Children with Campylobacter-associated diarrhoea were younger than controls (OR 0.93, 95% CI: 0.90-0.97, p<0.001), more likely to have household adult(s) with diarrhoea in the previous week (OR 7.02; 95% CI 1.20-40.94, p=0.02) and to have Campylobacterpositive environmental samples (OR 6.674; 95% CI 1.530-29.11, p=0.01). Absence of a dedicated food preparation area was associated with increased risk (OR 0.07; 95% CI 0.01-0.74, p=0.01).
CONCLUSION
Campylobacter-associated diarrhoea in children is strongly linked to adult illness and environmental contamination, implicating person-to-person and environmental transmission within the household. Targeted improvements in household hygiene practices, particularly dedicated food preparation areas, represent actionable interventions to reduce Campylobacter-associated diarrhoea in children in this setting.

abstracts.Abstract title: SHARED AND SITE-SPECIFIC IMMUNE ARCHITECTURE ACROSS HUMAN NASAL AND FEMALE GENITAL TRACT MUCOSA 1 1 1 1 1 Ndaru Jambo , Edwin Lisimba , Alice Kusakala , Chisomo Kafamau , Bridget Ibbu , George
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Mucosal immunity; tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM); Female genital tract; Nasal mucosa; Spectral flow cytometry
BACKGROUND
Human mucosal tissues serve as major portals of pathogen entry and important sites of immune defence. The common mucosal immune system theory proposes that immune responses induced at one mucosal site can influence immunity at distant mucosal surfaces. However, the extent to which distinct human mucosal tissues share common immune architecture or exhibit site-specific organisation remains poorly understood, particularly in settings with high pathogen exposure. We therefore sought to define the cellular, memory, and tissue-residency landscapes of the nasal and female genital tract (FGT) mucosa in adult women in Malawi.
METHODS
We collected paired samples of nasal mucosa (inferior turbinate curettage and nasopharyngeal swab) and FGT (endocervical brush and ectocervical swab) from HIV-uninfected adult women in Malawi (n = 15). High-dimensional spectral flow cytometry was performed using a 27-parameter panel to quantify and phenotype major immune cell populations, including T cells, B cells, natural killer (NK) cells, NKT cells, monocytes, and neutrophils. CD69+CD103+, CCR7-CD45RO+, CCR7+CD45RO+, CCR7+CD45RO-, and CCR7-CD45RO- cells were classified as tissue-resident memory (TRM), effector memory (TEM), central memory (TCM), naive (TN), and terminal effector memory RA (TEMRA), respectively.
RESULTS
Principal component analysis revealed both shared and site-specific features of mucosal immune architecture. Endocervical and ectocervical immune profiles clustered closely together, indicating a highly conserved immune landscape within the FGT, whereas nasal mucosal sites exhibited greater heterogeneity, with inferior turbinate profiles forming a distinct cluster and nasopharyngeal profiles partially overlapping with those of the FGT. The FGT was enriched for neutrophils and monocytes and contained fewer T cells than the nasal mucosa, while B cells were enriched in the nasopharynx and CD8+ T cells in the inferior turbinate. Among CD8+ T cells, TEM cells predominated across mucosal sites, although TCM cells were enriched in the endocervix. Distinct patterns were observed among CD4+ T cells, with TEM cells predominating in the nasal mucosa and TCM cells predominating in the FGT. Tissue residency phenotypes further distinguished mucosal sites, with nasal CD8+ T cells predominantly exhibiting a TRM phenotype, whereas FGT CD8+ T cells comprised both TRM and CD69+CD103populations. CONCLUSIONS The upper respiratory tract and FGT mucosa exhibit both shared and site-specific immune features, reflecting common mucosal immune architecture alongside local tissue adaptation. These findings provide a framework for generating hypotheses and advancing understanding of mucosal immunity in humans.

abstracts.Abstract title: IMPLICATIONS OF PNEUMOCOCCAL CARRIAGE, SHEDDING, ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE PATTERNS, AND POTENTIAL WITHIN-HOUSEHOLD TRANSMISSION IN MALAWI
abstracts.plainConclusion: Mothers shed pneumococci, often without detectable nasopharyngeal carriage, suggesting that carriage-based surveillance alone may underestimate transmission potential and underscoring the importance of incorporating shedding as a complementary measure in pneumococcal transmission and vaccine impact studies.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
BACKGROUND
Pneumococcal nasopharyngeal carriage is commonly used in transmission studies, but little is known about pneumococcal shedding as a surrogate for transmission. We investigated pneumococcal shedding and resistance patterns among pregnant and lactating mothers and potential within-household transmission to their children in Malawi.
METHODS
In an ongoing prospective, two-arm randomised PCV13 trial, pregnant women, their under-fives, and newborns were followed across three visits: baseline (antenatal), and 6-week and 9-month postnatal visits. We collected cough samples and nasopharyngeal swabs (NPS) from the mothers and only nasopharyngeal swabs from their children. Pneumococci were identified, serotyped, and tested for AMR using standard bacteriological methods. Interim findings on carriage and shedding (not by intervention) were evaluated.
RESULTS
A total of 1,690 paired cough and NPS samples from the three visits were analysed from 783 mothers. Pneumococcal carriage proportion was 19.64% while shedding was 10.11%. For the shed isolates, AMR prevalence was 90.5% for cotrimoxazole, erythromycin 38.0%, tetracycline 62.0% and benzylpenicillin 62.0% (MIC > 0.06 mg/L). Most shedding episodes occurred in the absence of detectable carriage (66.1%; 113/171). We identified six shed isolates from mothers without detectable carriage that shared similar serotypes as isolates recovered from their corresponding child within the same household (serotype 3, n = 3; serotypes 23A/23B, 19A, and 15, n = 1 each).
CONCLUSION
Mothers shed pneumococci, often without detectable nasopharyngeal carriage, suggesting that carriage-based surveillance alone may underestimate transmission potential and underscoring the importance of incorporating shedding as a complementary measure in pneumococcal transmission and vaccine impact studies.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
HIV, Alveolar Macrophages, Reservoirs, Epigenetic reprogramming RESEARCH CONTEXT Despite potent antiretroviral therapy (ART), an HIV cure remains elusive due to persistent viral reservoirs. While ART suppresses viral replication, treatment interruption leads to viral rebound. This is driven by infection of memory CD4+ T-cells and tissue-resident macrophages, which harbour long-lived virus. Most cure strategies have focused on resting CD4+ T-cells, with less focus on tissue-resident macrophages such as Alveolar Macrophages (AMs). AMs are long-lived lung immune cells that resist HIV-induced cell death through poorly understood mechanisms, enabling them to act as stable reservoirs. Like T-cells, macrophages support both productive infection and latency, but their infection dynamics differ. HIV infection alters the epigenetic landscape of both cell types, yet the role of these epigenetic changes in macrophage persistence remains unclear. Understanding this could reveal new approaches to eliminate HIV reservoirs. RESEARCH QUESTION & OBJECTIVE This study investigates how epigenetic reprogramming of lung-resident macrophages influences HIV replication, aiming to identify epigenetic compounds that restrict viral replication in an ex vivo human AM model.
METHODS
Chemical libraries of epigenetic modifiers (MedChemExpress and APExBio) were screened in HIV-infected AMs using a luminescent reporter virus to quantify replication. Alamar blue assays were used to detect cytotoxicity.
RESULTS
& CONCLUSION Across 12 assays, PARP1/2 and HIF inhibitors, along with PKC activators, reduced HIV replication by making AMs less permissive. PARP1/2 inhibitors showed selective cytotoxicity in infected cells. Bromodomain inhibitors were also identified as potential latency reversal agents. These findings highlight promising targets for disrupting HIV persistence in macrophages.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
BACKGROUND
Environmental surveillance (ES) of wastewater and rivers provides a cost-effective, population-level approach to pathogen detection with potential to inform vaccine deployment and impact evaluation. Shigella has been detected in environmental waters; however, it remains unclear whether environmental detection correlates with clinical shigellosis incidence or captures circulating species and serotypes.
METHODS
We implemented ES alongside the Enterics for Global Health (EFGH) hybrid Shigella clinical surveillance study in Ndirande, Blantyre (~103,000 residents) which drains into the Mudi River. Weekly samples were collected from nine river sites and one defunct wastewater treatment plant (n=530). Shigella-positive samples underwent speciation and serotyping using the same multiplex qPCR assays as EFGH clinical diagnostics, enabling direct comparison.
RESULTS
ipaH was detected in 22.1% of grab samples and 42.1% of Moore swabs. Mixed-effects regression using ipaH copy number from unenriched grab samples showed a statistically significant positive association with clinical incidence. S. sonnei was detected in only 3.1% of ES samples, indicating marked discordance requiring further investigation. Serotype resolution for S. flexneri was limited by mixed environmental populations; however, S. flexneri 6, the second most common clinical serotype, was detectable via a unique PCR target (29.7% Moore swab positivity).
CONCLUSION
Data suggests ES reflects population-level Shigella burden, though serotype-level detection requires further validation before ES can be used to guide vaccine introduction. If concordance between environmental and clinical serotype distributions is confirmed, ES could serve as a scalable, low-cost tool to monitor vaccine impact without reliance on facility-based surveillance alone.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
BACKGROUND
Despite widespread use of the infant 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13), vaccine-type carriage, particularly serotypes 3 and 19F, remains prevalent among adults in Malawi. However, the underlying genomic mechanisms driving this persistence and the relative contributions of clonal expansion versus capsular dissemination remain poorly understood.
METHODS
We conducted a longitudinal study among adults in Blantyre, Malawi, following participants weekly for the first month and then monthly for 12 months. Whole-genome sequencing was employed to analyse 477 pneumococcal genomes from 70 PLHIV on ART (301 genomes) and 37 HIV-uninfected (176 genomes) adults.
RESULTS
Serotypes 3 (8.5%) and 19F (7.4%) were the most common among the adults. Serotype 3 was associated with four distinct lineages (GPSC 3, 10, 56 and unassigned), and serotype 19F with five (GPSC 1, 10, 21, 192 and 202). Notably, we identified a strong positive correlation between serotype carriage frequency and lineage diversity (Spearman's rho = 0.53, p = 0.00016). Phylogenetic analysis of the capsular polysaccharide synthesis (cps) locus demonstrated that capsular diversity is highly structured by genetic lineage rather than random variation.
CONCLUSION
The extensive cps locus diversity observed in serotypes 3 and 19F underscores their strong adaptive capacity in the post-PCV13 era. Both serotypes circulate across multiple lineages, including the MDR-associated GPSC10, demonstrating ongoing evolutionary plasticity that could facilitate evasion of vaccine-mediated immune pressure.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Antimicrobial resistance, Antimicrobial stewardship, Dashboard, Digital Health
INTRODUCTION
Microbiology and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) data are critical for antimicrobial stewardship but remain underused in many low- and middle-income country hospitals, where results are siloed in laboratory information management systems (LIMS) and often reported as static periodic summaries. At Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital (QECH), Malawi, this delay in translating routine microbiology data into actionable insight has previously resulted in unrecognised outbreaks and emerging resistance trends.
METHODS
We designed and developed AMRtrack, an interactive AMR surveillance dashboard using a client-server architecture: a Python/Django backend extracts, validates, standardises (using LPSN bacteria nomenclature and EUCAST antibiotic naming) and aggregates culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing data from the QECH/MLW LIMS, exposing processed outputs via secure RESTful APIs to a React frontend. Development was informed by a needs assessment with clinicians, laboratory staff, and policymakers, with iterative stakeholder review throughout.
RESULTS
AMRtrack presents organism distribution, temporal resistance trends, and antibiotic resistance heatmaps with ward-, specimen-, and date-range filters, alongside a laboratory quality section tracking contamination and culture positivity rates. Applied to over 17,500 results, the dashboard enables real-time visualisation of organism-antibiotic resistance trends and drill-down exploration of specific combinations, functionality previously inaccessible through static reporting.
CONCLUSION
AMRtrack demonstrates a practical, open-source, replicable model for near-real-time AMR surveillance in resource-limited settings, addressing the gap between routine microbiology data generation and its use for clinical and public health decision-making.

KEYWORDS
Climate and health, Photovoice, Community engagement, Co-create solutions, community-led sensitisation
INTRODUCTION
Climate change has led to rising global temperatures, resulting in an increase in extreme weather events that adversely impact public health. Approximately 3.6 billion people worldwide are vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with developing countries being disproportionately affected despite their low carbon emissions. Malawi, for instance, was devastated by Tropical Cyclone Freddy in 2023, which caused the deaths of over 1,200 individuals, widespread displacement, injuries, and significant damage to infrastructure essential for delivery of healthcare services. This community engagement project adopted a bottom-up approach to understand the perspectives and lived experiences of individuals about the health impacts of climate change.
METHODS
Using photovoice, 40 community members were engaged to capture their experiences through photographs and personal narratives in Blantyre and Chikwawa districts. Data was analysed using content analysis.
RESULTS
Key emerging themes included an increase in communicable diseases, greater exposure to zoonotic diseases, water scarcity, infrastructure damage disrupting healthcare access and delivery, low crop yields, economic loss due to business disruptions, increased sexual violence and abuse, and rising mental health issues. Participants proposed community-led sensitization, community-led reafforestation, multisectoral collaboration and having active and up to date disaster preparedness and response plans to effectively mitigate effects of climate change.
CONCLUSION
The findings from this project aimed to enhance epistemic justice by co-creating working solutions with communities for strengthening resilience to withstand extreme weather events, advocate for policy change, and provide evidence to inform health research agendas that tackle the challenges faced by climate vulnerable communities.

abstracts.Abstract title: QUANTIFYING THE MALARIA BURDEN ATTRIBUTABLE TO ANTHROPOGENIC CLIMATE CHANGE IN MALAWI
abstracts.actualAbstract:
BACKGROUND
Malaria burden in Malawi has declined to below 5% prevalence, reviving prospects for elimination. However, a changing climate threatens these gains, as conditions suitable for transmission expand. Yet the contribution of climate change remains poorly quantified, with evidence drawn largely from correlational studies that cannot establish causation. This study aims to establish that causal link for Malawi, strengthening the evidence base for intervention planning.
METHODS
We obtained district-level malaria case data for 2004-2020 from DHIS2. Bias-corrected climate variables came from an ensemble of seven CMIP6 global climate models, generating factual and counterfactual scenarios. Factual simulations represent modelled historical trajectories of rainfall, temperature and relative humidity, while counterfactual simulations removed the anthropogenic warming signal to approximate a world without human-induced warming. We fitted distributed-lag non-linear models with a negative binomial distribution to estimate malaria incidence rate ratios under each scenario. Attributable fractions were then calculated at the district level to identify the highest-burden districts.
RESULTS
Preliminary results indicate that anthropogenic climate change has increased the malaria burden in Malawi, with clear heterogeneity between districts. Among the climatic drivers examined, rainfall emerged as the leading predictor, accounting for the largest share of attributable cases. The attributable burden was unevenly distributed across the country. Nkhotakota, Mulanje and Salima carried the highest burden, underscoring the localised nature of climate-driven malaria risk. CONCLUSIONS Achieving elimination requires quantifying the contribution of climate change so that climate-tailored interventions can be designed. This work provides a framework for establishing that causal link.

abstracts.Abstract title: ADVANCING HEALTH SYSTEMS RESILIENCE RESEARCH IN THE CONTEXT OF CLIMATE-INDUCED DISASTERS: EVIDENCE FROM KENYA, MALAWI, AND ZIMBABWE
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Climate-change, Health system resilience, Research agenda, preparedness, response, recovery
BACKGROUND
Increasingly recurrent climate-induced natural disasters force health systems to operate in continually precarious environments. Effective preparedness and response to persistent climate-induced disruptions require robust evidence to shape emergency preparedness, response and recovery strategies. We explored critical knowledge gaps within health systems resilience research to inform national research agendas on health system resilience in Kenya, Malawi, and Zimbabwe.
METHODS
A multiphase, mixed-methods study was carried out in Kenya, Malawi and Zimbabwe. Data were collected through a scoping review (n=133 articles), key informant interviews (n=54) and online survey (n=90) with policymakers, implementers, funders, and researchers. Data were coded inductively and deductively and analysed using the Blanchet (2017) framework on Dimensions of Resilience Governance.
RESULTS
Research questions spanned absorptive, adaptive, and transformative health system resilience capacities. Absorptive questions focused on maintaining essential mental health services, ensuring access to care, assessing climate impacts on health, and identifying country-specific indicators for monitoring preparedness, response, and recovery. Adaptive questions addressed strengthening early warning and response systems through predictive modelling, improving supply chains, climate-resilient infrastructure, and enhancing the health workforce's knowledge and skills to respond to climate-related emergencies. Transformative questions explored long-term recovery mechanisms, community engagement in planning and response, integration of social determinants of health to address vulnerability, and strengthening the resilience of commodity supply chains to withstand disruptions caused by climate-related shocks and stressors. CONCLUSIONS Addressing these climate-health knowledge gaps requires a strategically prioritised health systems resilience research agenda. Such an agenda will guide evidence-informed policy and strengthen preparedness, response and recovery in contexts of climate-induced health disasters.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
case cross over, PM2.5, WBGT, lag, preterm birth
BACKGROUND
Sub-Saharan Africa bears a disproportionate burden of global preterm births (PTB). While the chronic health impacts of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) are well-documented, localized multi-country evidence mapping its acute triggering effects and potential interaction with meteorological factors like Wet Bulb Global Temperature (WBGT) over PTB remains critically sparse.
METHODS
Utilizing a harmonized dataset from the HE2AT Centre spanning 2003-2023 across 8 African countries, we executed a time-stratified Case-Crossover Distributed Non-Linear Model (CC DNLM) to assess day-specific risks across an 8-day lag window (Lags 0-7) among 10,015 unique mothers with PTB. To investigate compounding hazards, individual records were aggregated into a daily time-series framework using a Generalized Additive Model with a quasi-Poisson log-link to estimate stratified interaction dynamics via a 2x2 exposure matrix and the Relative Excess Risk due to Interaction (RERI).
RESULTS
The CC DNLM revealed a highly compressed, immediate window of vulnerability. High PM2.5 exposure (76.83 ug/m3) was associated with a statistically significant 10.5% surge in the odds of PTB on the day of exposure (Lag 0: OR = 1.105, 95% CI: 1.016, 1.202), remaining elevated through Lags 1-2 before decaying. A conservative sensitivity analysis adjusting for continuous WBGT strongly replicated this acute temporal pattern (Lag 0: OR = 1.2478, 95% CI: 1.0887, 1.4303). In the interaction framework, acute heat stress independently increased daily risk (IR = 0.231%), but concurrent high exposures revealed a sub-additive, non-synergistic plateau (RERI = -0.001, 95% CI: -0.003, 0.001), dragging PM2.5 metrics into an inverse territory (IR = -0.156%).
CONCLUSION
Public health frameworks must transition from isolated environmental silos to compound risk models to protect vulnerable maternal populations amidst accelerating climate anomalies.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Infection prevention and control, healthcare associated infections, implementation science
BACKGROUND
Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a significant patient safety challenge in low-resource settings. Although Malawi has national infection prevention and control (IPC) guidelines, implementation remains inconsistent due to limited resources, inadequate training and weak monitoring systems. The IPC-Implement study aimed to develop and evaluate a context-specific, multifaceted implementation strategy to improve IPC practices in tertiary hospitals.
METHODS
We conducted a mixed methods implementation study at two tertiary hospitals from April 2023 to June 2026. The intervention was co-created and informed by formative research and the WHO multimodal IPC improvement strategy. The components included context-specific implementation strategies, community engagement and involvement, HAI point prevalence surveys and cost evaluation of the IPC intervention. Process outcomes included hand hygiene and aseptic technique compliance, while clinical outcomes were assessed using repeated HAI point prevalence surveys.
RESULTS
Baseline assessments demonstrated poor compliance with hand hygiene and aseptic techniques. Following implementation, hand hygiene compliance improved from 5.8% to 39.1%. HAI prevalence declined substantially, from 5.1% to 2.3% and 4.7% to 2.1%. Improvements were supported by strengthened leadership, increased availability of IPC resources, continuous audit and feedback and peer-topeer learning.
CONCLUSION
Findings suggest that a co-created, multifaceted implementation strategy can improve IPC practices and reduce HAI prevalence in resource-constrained hospitals. Integrating implementation strategies within routine hospital systems offers a promising approach for strengthening patient safety and informing national scale-up of IPC interventions in Malawi.

abstracts.Abstract title: UNDERSTANDING SEVERE MATERNAL INFECTIONS AND IMPACTING HEALTH OUTCOMES IN MALAWI: A MIXED-METHODS IMPLEMENTATION SCIENCE STUDY
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Severe maternal infection; implementation science; antimicrobial resistance; Malawi
BACKGROUND
Severe maternal infections (SMI) are a major cause of maternal mortality in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), including Malawi. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), limited surveillance data, and health system constraints impede timely diagnosis and appropriate management. This study investigated the epidemiology of SMI in Malawi and developed a theory-informed programme framework for infection prevention and management.
METHODS
A mixed-methods implementation science study comprised: (1) a systematic review and meta-analysis of maternal bacterial infections and AMR in SSA; (2) analysis of 11 months of baseline data (March 2023-February 2024) from the Active Prevention and Treatment of Sepsis Trial in Malawi to estimate SMI incidence and associated factors; and (3) retrospective development of a programme theory using behavioural science frameworks.
RESULTS
The systematic review (2,575 women) identified mixed-growth (17%) and E. coli (11%) as the predominant isolates, with AMR ranging from 19% to 77%. The median SMI incidence was 1,577 per 100,000 live births, peaking at 2,271 in July 2023. Increased risk of SMI was associated with the postnatal period, previous miscarriage or abortion, and inter-facility transfer. Service readiness deficiencies, including lack of ambulances (OR 4.1), limited glove availability (OR 2.3), and shortages of clindamycin (OR 2.6) and ciprofloxacin (OR 1.8), were significantly associated with SMI. The programme theory identified behaviour change techniques corresponding to these implementation barriers. CONCLUSIONS SMI in Malawi are associated with both clinical and health system factors. Integrating epidemiological evidence with implementation science provides a framework for infection prevention and management, improving service readiness, and informing maternal health policy in resource-limited settings.

KEYWORDS
Delayed ANC, Spatial inequalities, maternal health, DHS
BACKGROUND
Delayed antenatal care (ANC) initiation is a major public health concern in Malawi, increasing the risk of poor maternal and newborn outcomes. This study examined the prevalence, determinants, and spatial inequalities of delayed first ANC initiation among women of reproductive age.
METHODS
We conducted a secondary analysis of the 2015-2016 Malawi DHS involving 13,448 women. Delayed ANC initiation was defined as the first ANC visit after 12 weeks of gestation. Guided by Andersen's Behavioral Model, we used descriptive statistics, multivariable logistic regression, and GIS-based spatial analysis to assess prevalence, determinants, and geographic distribution.
RESULTS
Over 70% of women initiate ANC after 12 weeks of gestation. Women aged 25-34 years (AOR=0.84; 95% CI: 0.75-0.93) and 35-49 years (AOR=0.84; 95% CI: 0.72-0.98) were less likely to delay ANC than those aged 15-24 years. Higher education (AOR=0.63; 95% CI: 0.45-0.88) and higher wealth status (AOR=0.86; 95% CI: 0.75-0.99) reduced the odds of delayed ANC. Spatial analysis identified hotspots in the Central and Southern regions, while travel-time analysis showed poor access to health facilities in rural and remote areas. CONCLUSIONS Delayed ANC initiation in Malawi remains high and is influenced by socioeconomic and geographic factors. Targeted interventions addressing both individual and structural barriers are needed to improve timely ANC uptake and reduce regional inequalities in maternal healthcare access.

abstracts.Abstract title: EFFECTS OF MULTIPLE MICRONUTRIENT SUPPLEMENTATION ON HEMOGLOBIN LEVELS AMONG ANAEMIC ADOLESCENT GIRLS IN PUBLIC SECONDARY SCHOOLS IN BLANTYRE, MALAWI: A RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED TRIAL Mayamiko D. Kapulula
abstracts.plainConclusion: This project could support strengthening school-based nutrition interventions and contribute to national efforts to reduce anaemia among adolescent girls before pregnancy, thereby improving maternal and newborn health outcomes.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Multiple Micronutrient supplements, Adolescent girls, Anaemia
BACKGROUND
Anaemia remains a major public health challenge among adolescent girls in Malawi, with iron deficiency and multiple micronutrient deficiencies contributing to poor health, impaired cognitive performance, and increased risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes later in life. Although iron-folic acid (IFA) supplementation is the current standard intervention, it does not address the broader spectrum of micronutrient deficiencies common in this population. Multiple micronutrient supplementation (MMS) has demonstrated improved maternal and child health outcomes in several low- and middle-income countries; however, evidence among school-going adolescents in Malawi remains scarce.
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the effect of multiple micronutrient supplementation on hemoglobin levels among anaemic adolescent girls attending public secondary schools in Blantyre, Malawi.
METHODS
A school-based prospective randomized controlled trial is proposed involving 212 anaemic, non-pregnant adolescent girls aged 15-19 years. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either daily MMS or the standard iron-folic acid supplement for 12 weeks. The primary outcome will be change in hemoglobin concentration from baseline to 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes will include changes in serum ferritin, folate and vitamin A concentrations, as well as adherence and acceptability of supplementation. Data will be collected electronically using REDCap and analysed using R software following the intention-to-treat principle. EXPECTED OUTCOMES The study is expected to generate the first evidence from Malawi on the effectiveness and feasibility of school-based MMS among anaemic adolescent girls. The findings will contribute to implementation of Malawi's National Multi-Sector Nutrition Policy and Strategic Plan (2023-2030), which prioritizes reducing anaemia and micronutrient deficiencies among women and adolescent girls.
CONCLUSION
This project could support strengthening school-based nutrition interventions and contribute to national efforts to reduce anaemia among adolescent girls before pregnancy, thereby improving maternal and newborn health outcomes.
