abstracts.Abstract title: EXPERIENCES OF VULNERABLE MATERNITY SERVICE USERS IN MALAWI AND ZAMBIA 1 1 2 3 Mtisunge Joshua Gondwe , Chifundo Kondoni , Arnold Hamapa , Catherine Bamuya , Annie
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
vulnerability, maternity care, experiences, antenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care
BACKGROUND
Tailoring maternity care to the needs of vulnerable pregnant women may reduce adverse pregnancy outcomes and improve positive experience. This study aimed to explore the maternity care experiences of vulnerable women in Malawi and Zambia to inform the design of interventions that more effectively address their unique needs to improve their overall health and well-being.
METHODS
We employed a phenomenological qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and vignettes with 69 purposively selected women who were pregnant or had given birth within six weeks in rural and urban Malawi and Zambia (May-August 2024). Participants included adolescents aged 10-19, in early or child-headed marriages, experiencing homelessness and women with disabilities, mental health conditions, seeking asylum, and domestic violence survivors. Data were thematically analysed using NVivo.
RESULTS
Four themes captured the experiences and needs of women in vulnerable situations across antenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal care. Experiences varied by vulnerability. Adolescents and women with disabilities often delayed antenatal care because of stigma, fear of judgment, and pregnancy concealment, while their needs were frequently overlooked. Although some reported supportive interactions, many experienced stigma, blame, unmet needs, and inconsistent care. During childbirth, adolescents commonly faced informational neglect and non-consented care, contributing to fear, confusion, and delayed care-seeking. Participants also felt treated as burdens, with care that failed to uphold dignity and person-centred principles. Postnatal care was inconsistently delivered, with structural inequalities affecting access, quality, continuity, and experiences across vulnerable groups. CONCLUSIONS Maternity care experiences varied by vulnerability, underscoring the need for tailored, person-centred interventions to improve equitable maternal care.

abstracts.Abstract title: MEASURING WOMEN'S EXPERIENCES WITH MATERNITY SERVICES: DEVELOPMENT OF A FEEDBACK TOOL IN MALAWI 1 1 1 1 Chifundo Kondoni , Mtisunge Joshua Gondwe , Yamikani Chimwaza , Leonard Mndala , Annie

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Maternity services users, feedback tool, co-design, participatory approach, experiences
BACKGROUND
Maternity service user feedback is vital for improving care quality. In Malawi, generic tools limit insight into experiences. This study co-developed a maternity-specific feedback tool through participatory stakeholder engagement.
METHODS
A qualitative, consensus-driven study was conducted in Malawi through a two-stage process comprising a co-design workshop (July 2024) and a validation workshop (February 2025). The co-design workshop involved four steps: group discussions on tool content and delivery options; World Cafe sessions for iterative refinement of content and implementation strategies; gallery walks to review five proposed delivery modalities and assess feasibility and implementation challenges; and silent voting to select preferred options. The validation workshop followed a similar structure, with group discussions used to review and test the selected tool and propose revisions, followed by gallery walks for cross-group feedback and further refinement. All discussions and outputs were documented and audio-recorded to capture decision-making processes and rationales.
RESULTS
A total of 46 stakeholders (95% of those invited) participated in the co-design workshop and 39 (95%) in the validation workshop. The process led to the development of a maternity care feedback tool with 87 indicators covering antenatal (27), labour and delivery (28), and postnatal care (32). Indicators were organized into seven domains, including respectful care, communication, emotional support, access, continuity, quality of services, and overall satisfaction, and the tool was developed in paper and electronic formats.
CONCLUSION
A structured co-design and validation process generated a practical, consensus-based maternity feedback tool to improve care delivery in Malawi.

abstracts.Abstract title: PREDICTORS OF NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER DIAGNOSIS AND FUNCTIONING IN EARLY SCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN IN MALAWI (PRE-NDD STUDY)
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Neurodevelopmental disorder, diagnostic accuracy, prediction
BACKGROUND
Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) include attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism, epilepsy, and neuromotor impairments (NMIs). NDDs impact 18.3% <10yo globally, with >90% living in low-and-middle-income countries (LMICs). Current diagnostic tools are expensive, time intensive, and require specialised training. This impedes early detection, limiting opportunities for intervention when neuroplasticity is maximal, especially in LMICs. Early detection is vital, with early interventions minimising social, behavioural, and educational impacts. The Scalable Transdiagnostic Early Assessment of Mental Health (STREAM) team tested a novel tablet-based neurodevelopmental assessment with 2036 0-6yo in Blantyre. We will identify predictors of NDDs and functioning in early school age children, including STREAM scores.
METHODS
We are assessing a retrospective cohort of n=430 2.5-6yo from the STREAM study, now 5-8yo. We are conducting diagnostic assessments for NDDs (ADHD, autism, epilepsy, and NMI), and measurements of participation, early learning, and cognitive ability.
RESULTS
We will provide evidence of the diagnostic accuracy (DA) and predictive validity (PV) of STREAM scores to predict future NDDs and functioning. Our interim analysis at 65% (n=281) recruitment comprised 53.4% males (n=134) at mean 6.6yo with 85.2% (n=210) in primary education. We identified 9.6% (n=27) with 1+ NDD. Total STREAM scores had an AUC of 0.75 (95% CI 0.62-0.87) for NDDs and were significantly correlated with age-adjusted cognitive ability (r=0.53, 95% CI 0.35-0.66, P<0.001), school readiness (r=0.44, 95% CI 0.33-0.53, P<0.001), and participation (r=0.19, 95% CI 0.07-0.03, P=0.001). CONCLUSIONS The STREAM tool could offer a simple, affordable, standardised platform for earlier identification of NDDs and functional difficulties.

abstracts.Abstract title: MAPPING INTERVENTIONS ADDRESSING HIV CARE ENGAGEMENT AMONG MOBILE POPULATIONS IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA: A SCOPING REVIEW
abstracts.plainConclusion: Supporting mobile populations across the HIV care cascade requires differentiated service delivery that responds to their unique mobility patterns; however, robust evidence on effective interventions remains limited. abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
HIV; Mobile Populations; ART Engagement
BACKGROUND
Mobile populations in Sub-Saharan Africa experience a disproportionately high burden of HIV and face unique barriers across the HIV care cascade. Despite increasing recognition of mobility as a barrier to HIV care, interventions designed for mobile populations have not been comprehensively described. This scoping review aimed to map interventions addressing HIV care engagement among mobile populations in Sub-Saharan Africa.
METHODS
We conducted a scoping review following JBI methodology, searching five electronic databases and grey literature for studies published in English between 1 January 1990 and June 2026. Studies describing interventions addressing HIV care engagement among mobile populations in Sub-Saharan Africa were included.
RESULTS
Twenty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria, including randomized and cluster randomized controlled trials (n approximately 12), qualitative studies (n approximately 10), demonstration, pilot and feasibility studies (n = 3), with the remainder using mixed methods or unspecified designs. Studies were published between 2010 and 2026 and conducted predominantly in Kenya and Uganda (n = 20), with fewer from Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia and South Africa. Interventions included community-led ART delivery, peer support, dynamic choice models, facility-led case management, and assessments of preferences for long-acting injectable ART. Evidence on intervention effectiveness was mixed, particularly for viral suppression, although interventions were generally well received.
CONCLUSION
Supporting mobile populations across the HIV care cascade requires differentiated service delivery that responds to their unique mobility patterns; however, robust evidence on effective interventions remains limited. Future research should evaluate and leverage differentiated service delivery approaches to better support continuity of HIV care among mobile populations.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI), Tuberculosis Prevention Therapy (TPT), Gender Responsive Health Care, Adult Tuberculosis Vaccination, Qualitative Research
BACKGROUND
In 2022, 43.9% of people in urban Blantyre had latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI), which can progress to TB disease and sustain transmission. TB preventive therapy (TPT) and emerging TB vaccines can reduce up to 50-90% progression from infection to disease, yet uptake remains low. This study explored how gender and age influence experiences, preferences, and uptake of TB infection testing, TPT, and potential TB vaccination among adolescents and adults in peri-urban Blantyre.
METHODS
In December 2025, we conducted age- and gender-specific focus group discussions with 38 purposively sampled participants from a previous TB infection prevalence survey in three high TB-burden communities. Visual participatory
METHODS
explored TB experiences, TPT preferences, and potential TB vaccine uptake. Data was analyzed using the Levesque conceptual framework for healthcare access.
RESULTS
Participants largely understood TB as a disease rather than a "silent" infection, with limited awareness of LTBI and TPT. Community-based TB testing was generally accepted, although stigma, misconceptions about blood testing, and fear of testing positive remained barriers. Gender and age influenced access: women and adolescents often required permission from spouses or guardians, while men frequently prioritized work over TPT. Participants preferred simplified TPT delivery, particularly long-acting injections, and viewed the absence of an adult TB vaccine as contributing to the ongoing TB burden.
CONCLUSION
Limited awareness of LTBI, stigma, and gender- and age-related barriers may reduce uptake of TB prevention interventions. Community engagement, person-centered care, and gender-responsive approaches are needed to improve TPT uptake and support future implementation of adult TB vaccines.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Dried spot, central nervous system, meningitis, Target Product Profile, diagnostic tools
INTRODUCTION
Timely diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) infections remains challenging in low- and middle-income countries due to poor laboratory infrastructure, lack of cold chain systems and reliable electricity. Dried spot technology offers a promising fit-for-purpose alternative by making the collection, storage and transportation of clinical specimens for the diagnosis of meningitis simpler, safer and more accessible. Here, we describe the development of a Target Product Profile (TPP) for a dried spot kit (DSK) informed by stakeholders' perspectives.
METHODS
A formative mixed-methods study was conducted, comprising an online survey administered to 110 respondents and semi-structured interviews conducted with 15 health-care workers from Chiradzulu, Chikwawa, and Blantyre districts in Malawi. Data was collected between October and December 2023. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, while qualitative data were analysed using thematic analysis. Participatory workshops explored engineering requirements and resolved outstanding TPP characteristics.
RESULTS
There was a high acceptance of the DSK, a strong need for training before implementation, and key requirements included affordability, paper card configuration, need for low limit of detection of 50 copies/mL of cerebrospinal fluid, broad pathogen compatibility including Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae and ambient storage compatibility.
CONCLUSION
The findings underscore a critical unmet need for a low-cost, robust, and user-friendly DSK to enable timely diagnosis and effective linkage to care for meningitis in low-resource settings. By directly addressing key barriers to specimen transport and diagnostic access, the proposed innovation has the potential to strengthen clinical decision-making, improve patient outcomes, and enhance surveillance capacity.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Radiology, Teleradiology, System-usability, QECH, Malawi
INTRODUCTION
Teleradiology has emerged as an important service delivery model for expanding diagnostic capacity in low-resource settings by improving access to specialist radiology expertise. To support CT reporting between Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital (QECH), Malawi, and Worldwide Radiology (WWR) volunteers, UK, the partners adopted a cloud-based image sharing platform, Collective Minds Radiology (CMRAD, Sweden). The usability of such platforms is fundamental to how effectively healthcare professionals use teleradiology within routine clinical workflows and realize its intended service delivery benefits. Therefore, evaluating platform usability helps identify implementation challenges and select teleradiology platforms that are fit for purpose in resource-constrained radiology settings.
METHODS
A mixed-methods study was conducted among radiologists, radiographers and radiology trainees. Quantitative data were collected using the System Usability Scale (SUS), while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews. SUS data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, interview data were analyzed thematically, and the findings were integrated through triangulation.
RESULTS
Fifteen participants completed the SUS questionnaire. The platform achieved a mean SUS score of 80.8 +/- 10.1, indicating excellent usability. Mean SUS scores were 78.3 for WWR radiologists, 80.8 for radiology trainees and 85.8 for QECH radiology staff. Participants described the platform as intuitive and easy to use, while identifying internet connectivity, limited interoperability and access to patient clinical information as the main challenges.
CONCLUSION
The CMRAD platform demonstrated high usability across all user groups. Its successful use depended not only on the platform itself but also on the infrastructure and workflows that supported it, guiding the implementation of teleradiology services in similar settings.

abstracts.Abstract title: SHIGELLA BURDEN, SEROTYPES AND ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE AMONG CHILDREN UNDER FIVE IN LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME COUNTRIES: THE ENTERICS FOR GLOBAL HEALTH STUDY
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Shigella, diarrhoea, antimicrobial resistance, vaccine, surveillance
BACKGROUND
Shigella is a leading cause of dysentery and diarrhoea in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with impacts on child health including environmental enteric dysfunction and growth impairment. We estimated the burden, serotypes, and antimicrobial resistance of Shigella-attributed diarrhoea in young children to inform vaccine trial planning.
METHODS
The Enterics for Global Health (EFGH) study was a prospective, facility-based surveillance study conducted from June 2022 to August 2024 across seven countries (Kenya, Malawi, Mali, The Gambia, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Peru). Children aged 6-35 months presenting with acute diarrhoea were enrolled. Shigella attribution was based on culture or qPCR (ipaH Ct <=29.5) from rectal swabs. Incidence was adjusted for care-seeking using population enumeration and healthcare utilisation surveys. Antimicrobial resistance was assessed by disc diffusion.
RESULTS
Among 9,476 enrolled children, Shigella was detected in 881 (9.3%) by culture and 1,870 (20.0%) by qPCR (of 9,354 tested). S. flexneri predominated, with serotypes 2a and 6 most common. Adjusted incidence ranged from 2.7 to 11.7 per 100 child-years by culture and 3.5 to 26.9 by qPCR across sites. Resistance to WHO-recommended antibiotics varied by site: ciprofloxacin 37.2% (range 14.0-74.0), azithromycin 22.1% (1.2-34.2), and ceftriaxone 16.2% (0.0-64.4). CONCLUSIONS Shigella-attributed diarrhoea remains common among young children in LMICs, with substantial antimicrobial resistance. Leading quadrivalent vaccine candidates cover most identified serotypes. These findings support the need for Shigella vaccines and demonstrate EFGH site readiness for vaccine trials.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Community-acquired pneumonia, Antimicrobial resistance
INTRODUCTION
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in pneumonia is a global health problem. Understanding how AMR develops and influences health outcomes in resource-limited settings can inform more effective control strategies. Nasopharyngeal carriage of pneumonia pathogens is a pre-requisite for infection. This study will examine whether antibiotics and hospitalisation for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) change nasopharyngeal AMR carriage in Malawian children.
METHODS
This observational cohort study is recruiting 92 outpatient children with CAP and 92 hospitalised children with CAP in Blantyre, Malawi. Nasopharyngeal swabs are being collected at recruitment and 3-month study visits for culture and metagenomic sequencing. Co-morbidities, pneumonia severity, antibiotic exposure and health outcomes are being recorded.
RESULTS
To date 92 outpatient CAP and 61 hospitalised CAP participants have been recruited; the median age is 19 (range 12-35) and 23 (12-36) months in respective groups. 50 (54%) of outpatient CAP and 36 (59%) of hospitalised CAP participants are male. Reported prevalence of pre-healthcare antibiotic use in outpatient (31.5%) and hospitalised CAP (27.9%) participants was similar, mostly amoxicillin or co-trimoxazole, for a median duration of 3 days. Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage was lower in hospitalised (45%) than outpatient CAP participants (79%), which may reflect true antibiotic exposure. There was no seasonal variation in pneumonia severity amongst hospitalised CAP participants (Fisher's Exact, p = 0.2). Reported prevalence of co-morbidities in outpatient (3.3%; bronchitis) and hospitalised CAP (1.6%; asthma) participants was similar.
CONCLUSION
This study will define nasopharyngeal AMR carriage in Malawian children with CAP, through antimicrobial susceptibility testing and metagenomic sequencing.

abstracts.Abstract title: LOT QUALITY ASSURANCE SAMPLING AS A TOOL FOR ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE SURVEILLANCE IN MALAWI
abstracts.plainConclusion: AMR LQAS is a feasible tool for decentralized AMR surveillance, supporting empirical treatment decisions and district-level health planning, while complementing Malawi's existing sentinel surveillance system.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Fever, LQAS, AMR Prevalence, bacterial carriage, ESBL
BACKGROUND
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is projected to cause 4.5 million deaths in Africa by 2050. In Malawi, WHO-recommended AMR sentinel surveillance is hospital-based, resource intensive, and lacks nationwide coverage. This study adapted Lot Quality Assurance Sampling (LQAS), a low-cost approach with typically small sample sizes for AMR surveillance at primary healthcare level.
METHODS
A cross-sectional study was conducted in 27 Health Centres (HCs) across urban Blantyre (10), peri-urban Blantyre (7), and rural Chikwawa (10). Using adapted LQAS AMR thresholds of 20% (upper) and 5% (lower), and misclassification probabilities of alpha=0.05 and beta=0.10, the study classified the three districts relative to have exceeded the allowable AMR prevalence for three bacterial pathogens and five antibiotics. Clinical management of 169 febrile children underfive was observed (urban Blantyre=6 per HC, peri-urban Blantyre=7 per HC and Chikwawa=6 per HC), and nasal and rectal swabs were collected for microbiological analysis.
RESULTS
Among 111 bacterial isolates identified, 63.0% were ESBL-producing E. coli, 9.9% ESBL K. pneumoniae, and 27.0% MRSA. ESBL E. coli and MRSA carriage exceeded the 20% threshold in all districts. ESBL E. coli showed high resistance to ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and co-trimoxazole in all districts, while resistance to meropenem and chloramphenicol remained below 20%. MRSA resistance to gentamicin and tetracycline was below 20% across all districts whereas resistance to erythromycin and co-trimoxazole exceeded 20% in urban and rural settings respectively.
CONCLUSION
AMR LQAS is a feasible tool for decentralized AMR surveillance, supporting empirical treatment decisions and district-level health planning, while complementing Malawi's existing sentinel surveillance system.

abstracts.Abstract title: BEYOND KNOWLEDGE: ATTITUDES AS A PATHWAY TO RABIES-SAFE PRACTICES IN URBAN LILONGWE, MALAWI
abstracts.plainConclusion: Rabies KAP levels were insufficient to support Zero by 30 goals. Findings suggests that information alone may not produce sustained preventive behaviour; rabies programmes should combine education with attitude-focused behaviour-change strategies.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
Rabies; dog-mediated rabies; knowledge, attitudes and practices; Malawi; mediation analysis
BACKGROUND
Rabies remains a neglected preventable cause of death, with domestic dogs responsible for nearly all human cases. Although mass dog vaccination is central to elimination, gaps in community engagement and preventive behaviour limit progress in many endemic settings. This study assessed rabies knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) across urban Lilongwe, Malawi, and examined whether attitudes mediate the relationship between knowledge and rabies-safe practices.
METHODS
We conducted a cross-sectional household survey across 12 residential areas in Lilongwe City between March and May 2020. A questionnaire was administered to 392 household heads. Knowledge, attitude and practice scores were expressed as percentages and classified as poor, average, or good. Associations with sociodemographic characteristics were assessed using chi-square tests and multivariable linear regression. Bias-corrected bootstrapped mediation analysis tested whether attitudes mediated the knowledge-practice relationship.
RESULTS
Mean scores were low for knowledge (38.93% +/- 15.89) and attitudes (29.99% +/- 14.68), but higher for practices (66.66% +/- 16.57). Most respondents had poor knowledge (79.3%) and attitudes (91.1%), while practice scores were more evenly distributed. Tertiary education and dog ownership were positively associated with knowledge, attitudes and practices, with tertiary education the strongest correlate across all three domains. Attitudes partially mediated the knowledge-practice relationship, with an indirect effect of b = 0.167 (95% BCa CI: 0.114-0.233), accounting for 46.1% of the total effect.
CONCLUSION
Rabies KAP levels were insufficient to support Zero by 30 goals. Findings suggest that information alone may not produce sustained preventive behaviour; rabies programmes should combine education with attitude-focused behaviour-change strategies.

abstracts.Abstract title: HISTIDINE-RICH PROTEIN 2 AND CLINICAL PREDICTION MODEL TO DETERMINE AETIOLOGY OF COMA IN MALAWIAN CHILDREN WITH DISCORDANT MALARIA DIAGNOSTICS
abstracts.plainConclusion: This clinical prediction model can better define aetiology of febrile coma, without reliance on sophisticated laboratory pfHRP-2 assays; crucial for clinicians managing these critically unwell cases in diagnostically limited, rural African settings.
abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
PfHRP2, cerebral malaria, non-malarial coma, ELISA
BACKGROUND
Febrile coma is a major cause of pediatric hospitalization and mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, with cerebral malaria (CM) being the leading cause. The diagnosis of cerebral malaria relies on the detection of Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia by microscopy and the detection of P. falciparum histidine-rich protein 2 (PfHRP2) using malaria rapid diagnostic tests (mRDTs). However, discordant malaria test results (microscopy-negative but mRDT-positive) may reflect either recently treated malaria or asymptomatic parasitemia, creating a diagnostic uncertainty. We aimed to improve the diagnostic accuracy of cerebral malaria among children with discordant malaria test results in resource-limited settings. METHODOLOGY This was a sub-study that recruited 429 children (<15 years old) presenting with coma at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital in Blantyre, Malawi between February 2018 and December 2020. All eligible children underwent malaria microscopy, mRDT testing, and plasma pfHRP2 quantification by ELISA. These data were combined with clinical and laboratory data to generate a diagnostic model.
RESULTS
73 children were classified as non-malarial coma (microscopy- and mRDT-negative), 224 as confirmed CM (microscopy- and mRDT-positive), and 132 had discordant malaria test results. Using plasma PfHRP2 as the reference standard, we developed a clinical prediction model that combined platelet count and retinopathy status as strong predictors of CM, with accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of over 88%.
CONCLUSION
This clinical prediction model can better define aetiology of febrile coma, without reliance on sophisticated laboratory pfHRP-2 assays; crucial for clinicians managing these critically unwell cases in diagnostically limited, rural African settings.

abstracts.actualAbstract:
KEYWORDS
generative AI, ODK, XLSForm, electronic data capture, data management
INTRODUCTION
Electronic data capture with Open Data Kit (ODK) underpins many health studies in Malawi, yet converting paper questionnaires into ODK XLSForms remains manual, slow, and error-prone, demanding specialist knowledge of XLSForm structure, skip logic, and ODK's restrictive XPath dialect. We developed ODKForm GenAI, a web-based system that uses generative artificial intelligence to automate this conversion while keeping a human in the loop.
METHODS
The system accepts questionnaires as PDF, Word, OpenDocument, spreadsheet, image, or text files. A Python service extracts content using PyMuPDF and optical character recognition; a large language model (Azure OpenAI, deterministic settings) then generates a structured form schema and enriches it with skip logic, constraints, and groups. Quality control is layered: structural validation with automatic repair, ODK-specific XPath expression checking, and pyxform validation. A web editor provides drag-and-drop editing, natural-language refinement, respondent preview, version history, and role-based access before export to XLSForm (.xlsx).
RESULTS
In internal testing with 31 research questionnaires (2,017 questions), the pipeline generated complete draft XLSForms in a median of 2.4 minutes per document, against a typical four-week departmental turnaround for manual form development. Twenty-three raw AI drafts (74%) passed pyxform validation without any manual correction, and the median number of manual edits and natural-language refinements per form was zero.
CONCLUSION
Generative artificial intelligence, combined with layered validation and human review, can substantially reduce the time and specialist expertise required to build ODK forms, strengthening data-collection capacity for research teams in low-resource settings. A formal evaluation of accuracy, correction effort, and usability is planned.
